People need to understand that requirements for junior positions aren't for full competency in the list of skills they request. They want you to at least be familiar but not proficient enough to where they can leave you on your own from day 1 and let you get on with it. From personal experience, most people ask is for you to COMMUNICATE. It's a lacking skill a lot of developers start with that never address it. It's important as a developer to reach out for help...especially as a junior developer because it is to be expected at that level, and good companies offer resources to help you get acquainted with the stack the company uses, and if they don't just ask.

n the 1980s I began to hear the term “paperless office”. It probably was used earlier than that, but I was too young to care. In the 90s I was a consultant/project coordinator. I saw a lot of offices, and a whole lot of paper. We had email. I used to print my emails out so that I could read them on the plane or in my hotel room. Printer technology was amazing. Computer screens were not so great for reading. It seemed that the offices were using more paper than ever. Paperless offices were a joke. In the 2000s, screens got much better. There were smart phones. Then tablets. Even early e-ink readers. At the end of that decade I was working at a metals factory in Hereford, UK. In the tour of the facility, my colleague pointed to a multi-story building (with an elevator) that he said used to be where they stored and processed their paper records. All of those records were now stored electronically, and the building was let out to other businesses. I was there to help design/implement a new system to replace the system that eliminated all those records.

I think people who use Chat-GPT to offload their thinking will get dumber. What I find fascinating is that it's not good enough yet to be able to actually do that though. You have to think critically to produce good output. You can't just copy paste your way through life with AI (yet). For software, the AI can write a lot of decent code now, but you still have to think pretty critically at a higher level. It's just adding more abstraction to the process, but still requires effort and thinking.

Putting aside "Will AI Take Your Job" , we know AI will take jobs that don't yet exist, which is a larger impact. Once you do the math over the next 20 years, you realize the workforce will grow by about 1 Billion individuals, many in developing countries. But AI will consolidate between 400-800 million jobs. Lets be conservative and call it 400 million. That includes jobs that are yet to exist and are yet to be added to your list of jobs. After a while you realize your job might not be eliminated, you simply won't be replaced when you leave the industry even as the population grows. There will be an "Entry Barrier". This creates a stagnation in the middle class, the tax base will shrink, a rise in youth unemployment, and countries will need to spend more even with a shrinking tax base on social safety nets. So the larger question is how will we, as a population, fund economies where the labor force outnumbers the number of available jobs?
